extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor advocates, attorneys, and policymakers involved in FLSA worker classification
extracted.subtask_short: FLSA employee vs independent contractor analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the multifactor 'economic reality' test under the Fair Labor Standards Act to determine whether a worker is an employee (economically dependent) or an independent contractor (in business for themself). Focuses on how to weigh factors, what facts to consider, and alignment with judicial precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence as the ultimate inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic dependence is the ultimate inquiry: an employee is someone who, as a matter of economic reality, is economically dependent on an employer for work—not for income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the analysis on whether the worker depends on the employer for work (opportunities/assignments), rather than merely whether the worker derives income from other sources. This is the touchstone that should inform consideration of each economic reality factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances multifactor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the multifactor economic reality test considering the totality of the circumstances rather than elevating any single factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess all relevant facts together; no one factor or set of factors is determinative. The test should be applied flexibly and holistically to reflect the economic reality of the whole activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not predetermine factor weights ('no core factors')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not designate any factors (e.g., control or opportunity for profit or loss) as universally 'core' or 'most probative' with greater weight across all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical rules that give predetermined weight to particular factors. Even when two factors point the same way, stronger factual findings under other factors can outweigh them. Courts have repeatedly cautioned against assigning specific, invariant weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all relevant facts; do not exclude facts from consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: All facts that are relevant to economic dependence should be considered; rules that preclude certain facts from being analyzed under the factors improperly narrow the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts may legitimately inform multiple factors (e.g., ability to work for others may be relevant to exclusivity and to opportunity for profit). The Department prefers a flexible approach that allows facts to be considered where they illuminate the economic reality, rather than rigidly limiting which facts fit under which factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'dependence-for-work' from 'dependence-for-income'
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis should generally follow the 'dependence-for-work' approach — whether the worker is dependent on the employer for work — rather than a 'dependence-for-income' approach that focuses on other income sources or wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some courts have used a 'dependence-for-income' lens, the Department and most courts historically analyze whether the worker depends on the employer for opportunities to work (i.e., business opportunities), which better aligns with the economic dependence inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor: focus on employer's right to control, not only worker's actual control
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing 'control,' consider the nature and degree of control over the work — emphasizing the employer's right to direct or supervise the work rather than only the worker's actual day-to-day exercise of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe control narrowly (e.g., only as the worker's exerted control). The Department cautions against equating the control factor with a common-law control test and against giving it dispositive weight, but still regards employer control as a legitimate part of the multifactor analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss factor: analyze correctly, not limited to worker initiative/investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze opportunity for profit or loss in the context courts have used it — not recast solely as worker initiative or investment indicating independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2021 IC Rule's reframing (treating investment/initiative only as part of this factor) was criticized; the Department favors treating opportunity for profit or loss in its broader, case-law-informed sense and not as a short-hand for independence based only on some investments or initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider integrality/centrality and permanence where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider facts such as whether the work performed is central or integral to the potential employer's business and the permanency/length of the working relationship as potentially probative factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong findings under factors like permanence or integrality may outweigh weaker findings under other factors. The Department warns against excluding these facts from consideration, as doing so can unduly narrow the Act's protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to address modern and technological work arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic reality test should be flexible and adaptable to modern work arrangements (including app-based and technology-facilitated relationships), not rigidly limited by an outdated weighting of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the multifactor test examines the whole activity and does not presume which aspects are most probative, it can be applied across traditional and emerging industries. The Department believes this flexibility better addresses changes in the economy than rigid factor hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with statutory text and judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Align the interpretive approach with the FLSA's text as interpreted by courts and with decades of case law applying the multifactor economic reality test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulatory formulations that are inconsistent with Supreme Court and appellate guidance (e.g., warnings against mechanistic application). The Department finds no statutory basis for predetermined factor weighting and declines to adopt approaches that narrow the Act's expansive definitions of 'employ,' 'employee,' and 'employ.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or formulaic application
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply the economic reality test in a mechanical, formulaic fashion (e.g., by assigning fixed weights or deterministic rules based on isolated factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal appellate courts have cautioned that it is impossible to assign specific and invariably applied weights to the factors. Analyses should be fact-driven, contextual, and recognize that different combinations of factors can lead to different outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appellate case law faithfully; do not overread cases to create universal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on appellate decisions, do not extract or recharacterize isolated language to justify universal rules that the courts themselves have not adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department found that cases cited in support of 'core factor' elevation do not, in fact, establish a universal rule favoring those factors. Regulatory analysis should avoid simplifying courts' nuanced, fact-specific reasoning into presumptive doctrines.
